title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
premise: At a lily-pad pond, Mira wants a grand concert for the frogs, Tom wants to win the ridiculous Golden Tadpole Spoon, and Pip the frog wants one quiet song for a neighbor. A floating reed stage, a ribbon of lanterns, and a silver kettle-drum can make the concert splendid—but the children mistakenly assume the quiet neighbor cannot hear. Seed conditions decide whether the neighbor is shy, away, or secretly eager for music, changing what the performers prepare and what the concert becomes.
cast_and_props: Characters: Mira, an enthusiastic child who wants a dazzling concert and believes every good audience should cheer; Tom, a competitive child who wants the Golden Tadpole Spoon and believes the loudest finale wins; Pip, a frog who wants to perform a gentle moon-song for the quiet neighbor and knows the pond’s small sounds well. Optional persistent listener entity: Nella, the quiet neighbor behind the cattails, whose hearing and invitation state can differ by seed. Props: floating reed stage (reedstage), silver kettle-drum (drum), lantern ribbon (lanterns), Golden Tadpole Spoon (spoon), and a paper invitation (invitation). Shared setting: one pond edge with cattails, lily pads, and a small audience space.
kernels_and_interactions: 1. Desire and belief: Mira wants spectacle; Tom wants the Spoon; Pip wants a particular song for Nella. Belief slots include Mira.knows.nella.hears, Tom.knows.best_song, and Pip.knows.nella.invited. 2. Invitation and knowledge: Mira or Pip can observe Nella’s presence, tell another character, and deliver the invitation; Nella’s response changes the intended audience without mind reading. 3. Prop ownership and placement: the children transfer the drum, lanterns, and Spoon; floating props can be placed on the reed stage or kept beside the pond. 4. Performance and audience reaction: a loud finale, a soft moon-song, or a mixed concert sets concrete facts such as concert.style, audience.delighted, and spoon.awarded. 5. Character turn: Tom may trade the winning finale for Pip’s quiet song, or Mira may invite Nella into the audience; this is pivotal because it changes the final performance, not merely a score.
seed_parameters: Use the supplied seed to choose scalar initial conditions, not a route number. Vary 2–4 premise keys such as n​ella.presence (pond/cattails/away), n​ella.hearing (keen/muffled), invitation.owner (mira/pip), and tom.plan (loud/clever). Preserve every chosen value as an actual declared state key. The seed may also set which prop begins on the bank, whether the Spoon is available to award, and whether Pip already knows Nella enjoys soft music. These changes should alter what is wanted, understood, traded, made, or performed.
candidate_scenes: Aim for 16–20 candidates and 5–9 selected events. Suggested IDs: look_nella (observe Nella’s presence), notice_quiet (Pip observes the quiet neighbor’s condition), ask_mira (Mira tells Tom what she believes), invite_nella (transfer invitation or establish invited=True), hear_answer (Nella’s response becomes known), float_stage (move reedstage to pond.performance), hang_lanterns (place lanterns on stage), claim_drum (transfer drum to Tom or Mira), rehearse_roar (Tom establishes loud finale), rehearse_moon (Pip establishes soft song), tom_hears_pip (tell Tom Pip’s wish), choose_kind_finale (pivotal choice setting tom.agrees=True), call_concert (establish concert.started), perform_roar (concert.style=loud and audience reaction), perform_moon (concert.style=soft and audience reaction), perform_mixed (concert.style=mixed and audience reaction), award_spoon (Spoon ownership changes only after a qualifying performance), welcome_nella (Nella joins or listens from cattails), and lantern_close (a reusable bridge before endings). Reuse look_nella, float_stage, hang_lanterns, call_concert, and lantern_close across materially different paths. An inciting action must be call_concert only after an invitation, promised performance, or observed audience condition has established the problem.
constraints: Declare every slot before use; all state keys begin with an existing entity ID. Use 3–5 kernel families, scalar state only, and no abstract counters. Use observe, tell, and transfer at least once, with guarded access and ownership. Use 1–2 pivotal scenes only: choose_kind_finale and possibly welcome_nella. Mark ordinary setup scenes non-pivotal. The shared planner must prune actions that do not affect an outcome or pivotal turn. Goals should accept several concrete endings, for example concert.finished=True and one of concert.style in {loud, soft, mixed}; outcome_keys should include concert.style, audience.delighted, and spoon.owner or Nella’s final location. Catalog prose must include every candidate scene, with conditional variants for who is present, who knows what, and which style was performed. No character may speak as if they know Nella’s condition before observing or being told it.
different_endings: 1. Loud triumph: If Nella is away or Tom’s loud plan remains dominant, the drum booms, Tom receives the Golden Tadpole Spoon, and the final image is the Spoon wobbling like a tiny brass moon while frogs cheer. 2. Quiet welcome: If Nella is present with keen hearing and Pip’s wish survives, the performers play the moon-song; Nella steps from the cattails, and the final image is one lantern reflected beside her still, smiling face. 3. Mixed concert: If Mira learns Nella is listening but Tom still wants a finale, the group begins softly and ends with a playful drum ripple; the audience reaction is shared rather than a simple prize, and the final image is the reed stage carrying both a curled cattail and the shining Spoon. 4. Empty-but-tender concert: If Nella is away, Pip still performs the moon-song for the pond itself; Tom may keep or surrender the Spoon according to whether he accepts the kind finale. The last image is the invitation floating home on a lily pad, its ink sparkling under the moon. Each ending needs at least two prose variants, guarded by actual final facts rather than by a branch number.
